name: Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
description: Classification, naming, preparation, acidity, esterification, dehydration, oxidation, phenol ring reactions, Kolbe, Reimer–Tiemann, Williamson, ether cleavage

cards.definition: Alcohol: –OH on an aliphatic carbon (CH₃OH). Phenol: –OH on an aromatic carbon (C₆H₅OH). Ether: R–O–R / Ar–O–R (CH₃OCH₃).
Alcohols → detergents, phenols → antiseptics, ethers → fragrances; ethanol in wood-polishing spirit; sugar, cotton, paper contain –OH
One, two, three –OH groups: C₂H₅OH, ethylene glycol, glycerol
One, two, three –OH on the ring (phenol, cresol; catechol; pyrogallol-type)
–OH on a carbon attached to 1, 2, 3 other carbons
–OH on an sp³ carbon next to C=C; can be 1°, 2° or 3°
–OH on an sp³ carbon next to an aromatic ring; 1°, 2° or 3°
–OH on an sp² carbon of C=C (or aryl carbon): CH₂=CH–OH
Simple (symmetrical): both groups same (C₂H₅OC₂H₅). Mixed (unsymmetrical): different (C₂H₅OCH₃, C₂H₅OC₆H₅).
1°, 1° (allylic), 2° (benzylic), 3° (allylic)
Replace "e" of the alkane with "ol"; number from the end nearest –OH. Polyols keep the "e": ethane-1,2-diol

cards.text: IUPAC names: isopropyl alcohol = {{c1::propan-2-ol}}; isobutyl alcohol = {{c2::2-methylpropan-1-ol}}; tert-butyl alcohol = {{c3::2-methylpropan-2-ol}}; glycerol = {{c4::propane-1,2,3-triol}}.

cards.term: Table 7.1: common and IUPAC names of alcohols
cards.definition: Table 7.1
Prefix cyclo, –OH at C-1: cyclohexanol, 2-methylcyclopentanol
o-, m-, p-cresol = 2-, 3-, 4-methylphenol
Catechol (1,2), resorcinol (1,3), hydroquinone (1,4)
Hydrocarbon with an –OR / –OAr substituent; the larger group is the parent (alkoxyalkane)

cards.text: Ether names: CH₃OCH₃ = {{c1::methoxymethane}}; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ = {{c2::ethoxyethane}}; anisole = {{c3::methoxybenzene}}; phenetole = {{c4::ethoxybenzene}}.

cards.term: Table 7.2: common and IUPAC names of ethers
cards.definition: Table 7.2
4-Chloro-2,3-dimethylpentan-1-ol; 2-ethoxypropane

cards.term: C–O–H angle in methanol and why?
cards.definition: 108.9°, slightly less than tetrahedral: lone pair–lone pair repulsion on O

cards.term: Why is C–O in phenol (136 pm) shorter than in methanol (142 pm)?
cards.definition: (i) Partial double bond from lone pair conjugation with the ring (ii) sp² carbon

cards.term: C–O–C angle in methoxymethane and why?
cards.definition: 111.7°, slightly more than tetrahedral: repulsion between the bulky R groups; C–O = 141 pm

cards.term: Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes: rule followed?
cards.definition: Markovnikov: propene + H₂O/H⁺ → propan-2-ol
1. Protonation of alkene by H₃O⁺ → carbocation. 2. Nucleophilic attack of water. 3. Deprotonation.
(BH₃)₂, then H₂O₂ / OH⁻: propene → propan-1-ol (looks anti-Markovnikov), excellent yield
Boron attaches to the sp² carbon with more H atoms; OH later replaces B there
H.C. Brown (1959); Nobel 1979 shared with G. Wittig

cards.term: Reducing aldehydes and ketones to alcohols?
cards.definition: H₂/Pt, Pd or Ni, or NaBH₄ / LiAlH₄. Aldehyde → 1°; ketone → 2°.
LiAlH₄ → 1° alcohol (excellent yield)

cards.term: Commercial route from acids to alcohols, and why?
cards.definition: LiAlH₄ is expensive: convert acid to ester, then catalytic hydrogenation
Nucleophilic addition of R–MgX to C=O → adduct; hydrolysis → alcohol + Mg(OH)X

cards.term: Grignard product with HCHO, other aldehydes, ketones?
cards.definition: 1°, 2°, 3° alcohol respectively
Count the R groups the carbonyl carbon ends with: HCHO has 0 → R adds 1 → 1°. RCHO has 1 → 2°. R₂CO has 2 → 3°.

cards.term: Products (Example 7.2): catalytic reduction of butanal; propene + dil. H₂SO₄; propanone + CH₃MgBr then H₂O?
cards.definition: Butan-1-ol; propan-2-ol; 2-methylpropan-2-ol

cards.term: Primary alcohols from HCHO + Grignard (Intext 7.4): (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH and cyclohexylmethanol?
cards.definition: (CH₃)₂CHMgBr + HCHO; cyclohexylmagnesium bromide + HCHO

cards.term: Another name for phenol, and first source?
cards.definition: Carbolic acid; first isolated from coal tar (19th century)
Fuse with NaOH at 623 K, 320 atm → sodium phenoxide; acidify

cards.term: Trap: NCERT gives 300 atm in Ch 6 but 320 atm in Ch 7 for this. Which to write?
cards.definition: Either is accepted; remember 623 K and ~300 atm (high T and P because aryl C–Cl is unreactive)
Benzene + oleum → C₆H₅SO₃H; fuse with molten NaOH → phenoxide; acidify
Aniline + NaNO₂ + HCl (273–278 K) → benzenediazonium chloride; warm with water → phenol + N₂
Cumene (isopropylbenzene) + O₂ (air) → cumene hydroperoxide; dil. acid → phenol + acetone

cards.term: Why is the cumene process important?
cards.definition: Most of the world’s phenol is made this way; acetone is a valuable by-product

cards.term: Effect of chain length and branching on b.p. of alcohols?
cards.definition: More C: higher (van der Waals). More branching: lower (less surface area).

cards.term: Why do alcohols and phenols boil higher than ethers, hydrocarbons, haloalkanes of similar mass?
cards.definition: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding

cards.term: Boiling points of ethanol, methoxymethane, propane?
cards.definition: 351 K > 248 K > 231 K (similar masses 46, 46, 44)

cards.term: Why are lower alcohols miscible with water? Trend?
cards.definition: They H-bond with water; solubility falls as the hydrophobic alkyl/aryl part grows

cards.term: Increasing b.p. (Example 7.3): pentan-1-ol, butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, methanol?
cards.definition: Methanol < ethanol < propan-1-ol < butan-2-ol < butan-1-ol < pentan-1-ol

cards.term: Increasing b.p.: pentan-1-ol, n-butane, pentanal, ethoxyethane?
cards.definition: n-Butane < ethoxyethane < pentanal < pentan-1-ol

cards.term: How can alcohols act as nucleophiles and as electrophiles?
cards.definition: Nucleophile: O attacks, O–H bond breaks. Electrophile: protonated alcohol, C–O bond breaks.

cards.term: Reaction of alcohols and phenols with Na, K, Al?
cards.definition: Give alkoxides / phenoxides + H₂

cards.term: Which reacts with aqueous NaOH: alcohol or phenol?
cards.definition: Only phenol (→ sodium phenoxide + H₂O)

cards.term: Alcohols and phenols as Brönsted acids?
cards.definition: They donate a proton to a stronger base, forming alkoxide / phenoxide (conjugate bases)

cards.term: Acid strength order of alcohols, and reason?
cards.definition: 1° > 2° > 3°: alkyl groups (+I) push electron density onto O, reducing O–H polarity
Alcohols are weaker acids than water; so alkoxides are stronger bases than OH⁻ (NaOEt > NaOH)

cards.term: Why can alcohols also act as Brönsted bases?
cards.definition: Lone pairs on O accept protons

cards.term: Why is the O of phenol’s –OH slightly positive?
cards.definition: Resonance puts the O lone pair into the ring

cards.term: Why is phenol more acidic than alcohols? (2 reasons)
cards.definition: (i) sp² carbon is more electronegative, polarising O–H. (ii) Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised (charge delocalised); alkoxide charge is localised.
Negative charge delocalised onto o- and p-carbons

cards.term: Why is phenoxide more stable than phenol itself?
cards.definition: Phenol’s resonance structures involve charge separation; phenoxide’s do not

cards.term: pKa of phenol vs ethanol, and meaning?
cards.definition: 10.0 vs 15.9: phenol is about a million times more acidic (higher pKa = weaker acid)

cards.term: Effect of –NO₂ and –CH₃ on phenol acidity?
cards.definition: –NO₂ (EWG) increases acidity, most at o/p; –CH₃ (EDG) decreases it (cresols weaker than phenol)

cards.text: pKa values: o-nitrophenol {{c1::7.2}}; m-nitrophenol {{c2::8.3}}; p-nitrophenol {{c3::7.1}}; phenol {{c4::10.0}}; ethanol {{c5::15.9}}.

cards.definition: Propan-1-ol < 4-methylphenol < phenol < 3-nitrophenol < 3,5-dinitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol

cards.term: Why is picric acid a strong acid?
cards.definition: Three –NO₂ groups pull electrons and stabilise the phenoxide

cards.term: Intuition: why do EWGs at o/p help more than at m?
cards.definition: Phenoxide’s negative charge sits on o/p carbons; an NO₂ there can soak up that charge by resonance, at meta only inductively
With RCOOH or (RCO)₂O (conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst) or RCOCl (pyridine) → esters

cards.term: Why remove water in acid esterification?
cards.definition: The reaction is reversible; removing water pushes it forward

cards.term: Role of pyridine with acid chlorides?
cards.definition: Base that neutralises HCl, shifting equilibrium right
Introducing CH₃CO–: salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
Analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic

cards.term: Do phenols undergo C–O cleavage reactions?
cards.definition: Only with zinc; the others are alcohols only
Alcohol + conc. HCl + ZnCl₂: 3° → turbidity immediately; 1° → no turbidity at room temperature (2° in a few minutes)

cards.term: Why does turbidity appear in the Lucas test?
cards.definition: Alcohols dissolve in the reagent; the alkyl halides formed are immiscible
Alkyl bromide
Conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, anhyd. ZnCl₂ or alumina → alkene; ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K
Milder: butan-2-ol with 85% H₃PO₄ at 440 K; 2-methylpropan-2-ol with 20% H₃PO₄ at 358 K
3° > 2° > 1° (carbocation stability)
1. Protonation (ethyl oxonium ion). 2. Loss of water → carbocation (slow, rate-determining). 3. Loss of H⁺ → ethene.

cards.term: Insight: does ethanol really form a CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation?
cards.definition: A 1° carbocation is very unstable; for 1° alcohols the steps effectively merge (E2-like). Write NCERT’s 3 steps in exams; the carbocation route is real for 2° and 3°.

cards.term: How is dehydration equilibrium driven forward?
cards.definition: Remove ethene as it forms; the acid of step 1 is regenerated in step 3
C=O forms with cleavage of O–H and C–H: a dehydrogenation
Acidified KMnO₄ (strong)

cards.term: Oxidant to stop at the aldehyde?
cards.definition: CrO₃ in anhydrous medium

cards.term: Best reagent for 1° alcohol → aldehyde? What is it?
cards.definition: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate: CrO₃ + pyridine + HCl); e.g. but-2-en-1-ol → but-2-enal
→ ketones (CrO₃)
Resist oxidation; with strong oxidants/heat, C–C cleaves → mixture of acids with fewer C

cards.term: Heated Cu at 573 K on 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols?
cards.definition: 1° → aldehyde; 2° → ketone; 3° → alkene (dehydration)
"1° and 2° lose H₂; 3° loses H₂O" (no H on the carbinol carbon to lose)
Oxidised to methanal → methanoic acid (blindness, death). Treat with IV diluted ethanol: it swamps the enzyme so kidneys excrete methanol.

cards.term: Effect of –OH on the benzene ring?
cards.definition: Activates the ring and directs to o/p (resonance)
Mixture of o- and p-nitrophenol

cards.term: Why is o-nitrophenol steam volatile but p- is not?
cards.definition: o-: intramolecular H-bond. p-: intermolecular H-bond (associated molecules). Separated by steam distillation.
2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid), poor yield
Phenol + conc. H₂SO₄ → phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid; then conc. HNO₃

cards.term: Phenol + Br₂ in CS₂/CHCl₃ at 273 K?
cards.definition: Monobromophenols: p-bromophenol major, o- minor

cards.term: Why does phenol brominate without FeBr₃?
cards.definition: Strongly activating –OH polarises Br₂ itself
2,4,6-Tribromophenol: white precipitate

cards.term: Intuition: why solvent decides mono- vs tribromination?
cards.definition: Water ionises phenol to the super-activated phenoxide and polarises Br₂ further, so all o/p sites react; non-polar CS₂ keeps it gentle
Phenol + NaOH → phenoxide; + CO₂ then H⁺ → 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid)

cards.term: Why does Kolbe’s reaction use phenoxide, not phenol?
cards.definition: Phenoxide is more reactive, enough to attack the weak electrophile CO₂
Phenol + CHCl₃ + aq. NaOH → substituted benzal chloride intermediate → hydrolysis → salicylaldehyde (–CHO at ortho)
Kolbe adds CO₂ → –COOH. Reimer–Tiemann uses CHCl₃ → –CHO. Both go ortho.
Benzene + ZnO

cards.term: Oxidation of phenol with chromic acid? In air?
cards.definition: Benzoquinone (conjugated diketone). Air: slowly → dark quinone mixtures.

cards.term: Products with HCl–ZnCl₂, HBr, SOCl₂ (Intext 7.6): butan-1-ol; 2-methylbutan-2-ol?
cards.definition: 1-Chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane, 1-chlorobutane; 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane
1-Methylcyclohexene; but-2-ene (major, Saytzeff after rearrangement)

cards.term: Methanol: old name, old and modern production?
cards.definition: Wood spirit: destructive distillation of wood. Now: CO + 2H₂ over ZnO–Cr₂O₃, 200–300 atm, 573–673 K.
337 K; small amounts cause blindness, large amounts death; solvent for paints/varnishes, mainly to make formaldehyde
Invertase: sucrose → glucose + fructose. Zymase (yeast): glucose → ethanol + CO₂.
Anaerobic; zymase stops above ~14% alcohol; air oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid (spoils taste)
351 K; solvent in paint industry, making carbon compounds; modern industrial route: hydration of ethene
Commercial ethanol made undrinkable with CuSO₄ (colour) and pyridine (foul smell)
Acts on the CNS: impairs judgment, lowers inhibitions; high amounts cause nausea, unconsciousness, can stop breathing

cards.term: Ethanol + H₂SO₄ at 443 K vs 413 K?
cards.definition: 443 K: ethene. 413 K: ethoxyethane.

cards.term: Mechanism of ether formation from alcohol?
cards.definition: SN2: an alcohol molecule attacks a protonated alcohol, then loses H⁺

cards.term: Limits of acid dehydration for ethers?
cards.definition: Only for 1°, unhindered alkyl groups at low T; 2° and 3° give alkenes

cards.term: Why can’t bimolecular dehydration make ethyl methyl ether cleanly?
cards.definition: A mixture of three ethers forms (dimethyl, diethyl, ethyl methyl)
Widely used once; replaced due to slow effect and unpleasant recovery
R–X + R′–O⁻Na⁺ → R–O–R′ + NaX: SN2 attack of alkoxide on a 1° alkyl halide

cards.term: Why must the alkyl halide be primary in Williamson?
cards.definition: Alkoxides are also strong bases: with 3° halides only elimination occurs
2-Methylpropene only, no ether

cards.term: Right way to make t-butyl ethyl ether? (Example 7.6)
cards.definition: (CH₃)₃C–ONa + CH₃CH₂Cl (bulky part as alkoxide, 1° halide)
Use phenoxide + alkyl halide
Sodium 4-nitrophenoxide + CH₃Br; 4-bromonitrobenzene + CH₃ONa fails (aryl halide won’t do SN2)
Sodium salt of 3-methylpentan-2-ol + ethyl bromide (1° halide)
Alexander William Williamson (1824–1904), professor at University College, London (1849)
309.1 K, 307.6 K, 390 K: ethers ≈ alkanes; alcohols much higher (H-bonding)

cards.term: Why are ethers as water-soluble as alcohols of similar mass?
cards.definition: Ether O can accept H-bonds from water (ethoxyethane 7.5 g, butan-1-ol 9 g per 100 mL; pentane immiscible)
Excess HX under drastic conditions → two alkyl halides (via R–OH)

cards.term: Reactivity of HX in ether cleavage?
cards.definition: HI > HBr > HCl (conc. HI or HBr at high T)
Phenol + CH₃X: alkyl–O bond breaks (aryl–O is stronger)

cards.term: Why doesn’t phenol go on to C₆H₅I?
cards.definition: sp² aryl carbon cannot undergo nucleophilic substitution

cards.term: Mechanism of ether cleavage by HI (1°/2° groups)?
cards.definition: Protonation → oxonium ion; I⁻ attacks the less substituted carbon (SN2): the smaller alkyl becomes the iodide

cards.term: Ether with a tertiary group + HI?
cards.definition: The tertiary group becomes the iodide (SN1, stable 3° carbocation): (CH₃)₃COCH₃ → CH₃OH + (CH₃)₃CI

cards.term: SN1 steps in cleavage of t-butyl methyl ether?
cards.definition: Slow: loss of CH₃OH → (CH₃)₃C⁺. Fast: I⁻ attacks.

cards.term: Rule of thumb for ether + HI products?
cards.definition: 1°/2° groups: smaller group → R–I (SN2). 3° group: 3° → R–I (SN1). Aryl: always gives phenol.

cards.term: Products with HI (Example 7.7): benzyl phenyl ether?
cards.definition: Benzyl iodide + phenol

cards.term: Products (Intext 7.12): CH₃CH₂CH₂OCH₃ + HBr; C₆H₅OC₂H₅ + HBr; (CH₃)₃COC₂H₅ + HI?
cards.definition: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + CH₃Br; phenol + C₂H₅Br; (CH₃)₃CI + C₂H₅OH

cards.term: Effect of –OR on the benzene ring?
cards.definition: Activating, o/p-directing (like –OH)
Br₂ in ethanoic acid, no FeBr₃ needed: p-bromoanisole (90%) major
CH₃Cl / anhyd. AlCl₃ → 4-methoxytoluene (major) + 2-methoxytoluene
CH₃COCl / anhyd. AlCl₃ → 4-methoxyacetophenone (major) + 2- (minor)
Conc. H₂SO₄ + HNO₃ → 2- and 4-nitroanisole (4- major)

cards.term: Name reactions and tests of Chapter 7
cards.definition: Kolbe (phenoxide + CO₂): Salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann (phenol + CHCl₃/NaOH): Salicylaldehyde; Williamson (RO⁻ + 1° R′X): Ether R–O–R′; Cumene + O₂, then H⁺: Phenol + acetone; Hydroboration–oxidation: Anti-Markovnikov alcohol; Lucas test: 3° turbid at once; 1° none
